item.title: World shares are mostly higher as Democrats gain majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate
item.description: World shares were mostly higher Wednesday after the U.S. midterm election yielded majorities for the Democrats in both houses of Congress.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — U.S. stocks soared Wednesday after U.S. President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections. Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6 per cent for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569 points, or 3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4 per cent. Stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil also tumbled below US$95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices. Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington. “Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy. Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and in some instances trade. A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank. An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.” All told, the S&P 500 rose 119.70 points to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569.40 to 53,356.12, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 364.50 to 25,736.51. Here’s a look at some of the moves that rippled through financial markets: Trump Media and Tesla sank Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 24.5 per cent. Since briefly touching a peak of US$175 five years ago, it’s dropped to US$4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform. Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3 per cent, and SpaceX sank 3.8 per cent. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress. AI companies in general are under pressure Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general. Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the further build out of AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high. Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 3.1 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.9 per cent. Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips held up better. Alphabet rose 3.2 per cent, for example. The parent company of Google had tumbled to its worst loss ever last Thursday on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments. Military suppliers felt pressure A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran. That hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military, including drops of 6.9 per cent for Lockheed Martin, 4.5 per cent for Northrop Grumman and 2.6 per cent for General Dynamics. Oil prices tumbled, and green energy companies rose The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil plunging 8.7 per cent to US$94.62. That in turn hurt stocks of big oil companies, which had been rallying for much of the year. ExxonMobil fell 4.6 per cent, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.2 per cent. Falling oil prices usually hurt stocks of renewable-energy companies because they can lessen the incentive to switch to other energy sources. But Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar rose 4.6 per cent, and Enphase Energy climbed 3.7 per cent. Healthcare stocks and dollar stores also rallied A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a 10.3 per cent rise for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites. Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans who are struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, rose 9.6 per cent. Bond yields tumbled In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as oil prices dropped and took pressure off inflation. The move could also be a signal that investors see less risk of Washington piling more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control. Treasury yields had climbed through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the U.S. government’s big debt, along with high inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.88 per cent from 4.95 per cent late Tuesday. Stocks jumped in much of the world Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped two per cent in Paris, 2.2 per cent in Shanghai and 1.8 per cent in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4 per cent. ___ Stan Choe and David Mchugh, The Associated Press AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report from Hong Kong, and McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany.

item.title: First Nations Bank gets $15M investment from Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation
item.description: First Nations Bank of Canada has announced a $15-million investment by the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — First Nations Bank of Canada has announced a $15 million investment by the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation. The investment will see the Nation become one of the bank’s largest shareholders, with about a 10 per cent ownership stake. The Indigenous-owned chartered bank, the only one of its kind in Canada, says the investment marks the completion of a $50-million capital raise. The lender provides commercial and personal banking services including loans, mortgages and investments to both Indigenous and non-Indigenous clients. First Nations Bank of Canada said the investment will expand its lending capacity and help it pursue opportunities in Indigenous business, infrastructure and economic development. Bill Lomax, president and CEO of the bank, made the announcement while speaking at the Canadian Club in Toronto on Wednesday. “With the addition of Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation as a major shareholder, that founding vision is stronger than ever,” Lomax said in a news release. “Today, we are building a growing national bank, supported by First Nations and Indigenous shareholders from across the country, and well positioned to pursue the significant opportunities ahead.” Following the investment, the bank will be owned by 117 First Nations and Indigenous communities. “By becoming a major shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada, we are investing in an opportunity to build long-term wealth for our community with a partner who understands our needs and aspirations,” Chief Margaret Sault of Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation, said in the release. “Meaningful participation in the Canadian economy includes having ownership in the institutions that help drive and shape its future.” First Nations Bank of Canada operates 22 branches and service centres, while managing more than $1.6 billion in assets. Its trust subsidiary, FNB Trust, has $5.57 billion in assets under administration. --- Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

item.title: U.S. election results could mark a turning point for Canadian aluminum
item.description: The head of Canada’s aluminum industry says the U.S. midterm election results could mark a turning point in the trade dispute between Canada and the U.S.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The head of Canada’s aluminum industry says the U.S. midterm election results could mark a turning point in the trade dispute between Canada and the United States. Jean Simard, president and chief executive of the Aluminum Association of Canada, said Wednesday the election sent a clear message that American voters are frustrated with the economic impact of U.S. trade policies. The results could increase pressure on Washington to roll back tariffs, he said. Canada produces roughly 3.3 million tonnes of aluminum annually, exporting about 90 per cent of its output, according to Simard. The vast majority of those exports historically went to the United States, but U.S. tariffs of 50 per cent have prompted Canadian producers to redirect shipments to Europe, he said. Simard said he hopes the election results embolden lawmakers to challenge U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade policies and create new momentum for an agreement with Canada. “I’m certainly far more optimistic than I’ve ever been, because the signal is overwhelmingly clearer than I thought it would be,” he said. Meanwhile, in a post on X, Canadian Federation of Independent Business president Dan Kelly said he hopes the election results will push Washington toward a lasting trade deal with Canada. He said the results show the trade dispute has worsened affordability concerns in border states and the Midwest. Kelly added that 87 per cent of Canadian small businesses want an agreement reached as quickly as possible. But Andreas Schotter, a professor of international business at Western University’s Ivey Business School, said Canadian companies should not expect a dramatic shift in U.S. trade policy. “Even on the Democratic side, there’s a strong ‘America First’ notion,” he said. “For businesses, there’s no immediate change … I don’t see us all of a sudden going back to full CUSMA.” The Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement replaced NAFTA in 2020. Schotter pointed out U.S. President Joe Biden left most of the trade policies introduced during Trump’s first term in place. The first Trump administration imposed tariffs of 10 per cent on aluminum imports in 2018. Canada was initially exempt but faced the tariffs from June 2018 until May 2019, when the exemption was restored. Trump briefly reimposed tariffs on certain Canadian aluminum products in 2020, but the exemption was restored before Biden took office. That changed when Trump returned to the White House. The U.S. imposed tariffs of 25 per cent on Canadian aluminum in March 2025 before doubling them to 50 per cent on June 4, 2025. Simard said Canada’s three major primary aluminum producers — Rio Tinto, Alcoa and Aluminerie Alouette — initially continued fulfilling orders to American customers despite the tariffs before redirecting shipments to Europe. He said Canadian producers have exported roughly 800,000 tonnes of aluminum to Europe since March 2025, compared with about 100,000 tonnes over a comparable period under normal market conditions. Simard said the strategy has allowed the industry to maintain production without layoffs or production cuts. Blair Dickerson, president and chief executive of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said a change in the political landscape in Washington doesn’t guarantee an immediate change in U.S. trade policy. Still, she said the steel industry is encouraged by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s recent comments that Canada-U.S. trade talks are progressing, and that the government remains focused on getting a good deal for all Canadians. “Our priority remains clear,” Dickerson said. “We need a fair and predictable trading relationship so that the Canadian steel sector can compete and grow.” --- Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026.

item.title: Books about immigration policy, SNC-Lavalin up for National Business Book Award
item.description: Books about corporate crisis management, immigration policy and Canadian publishing are shortlisted for the National Business Book Award.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Books about corporate crisis management, immigration policy and Canadian publishing are shortlisted for the National Business Book Award. The annual $30,000 literary prize says it recognizes Canadian authors whose work demonstrates exceptional research, originality, and relevance to contemporary business challenges. The Globe and Mail columnist Tony Keller is shortlisted for “Borderline Chaos: How Canada Got Immigration Right, and Then Wrong” which analyzes immigration policies and how to move them forward. Longtime book publisher Scott McIntyre is nominated for “A Precarious Enterprise: Making a Life in Canadian Publishing,” which provides an insider’s view of the publishing business and its evolution. Rounding out the finalists is Lawrence Stevenson for “Inside SNC-Lavalin: How Crime and Politics Almost Killed a Great Canadian Company” in which the company’s former director and board chair shares an inside perspective of the corporate scandal. The winner will be announced on Nov. 26 at a ceremony in Toronto. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 4, 2026. Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press
